title: AcmeAI x Redwood - runtime performance deep dive (latency variance / long-context)
topics: Latency variance across GPU SKUs (L4 vs A10 vs A100/H100)
Long-context prefill vs decode behavior (8k-32k prompts)
Kernel selection logic (table-driven selector v2, fallback/overrides)
Observability: kernel_choice telemetry and correlation with p95
Dedicated vs Hosted deployment options; mixed-SKU fleets; MIG considerations
Benchmark methodology and next steps for a pilot
summary: AcmeAI described significant p95/p99 variance across GPU SKUs (especially A10 vs L4) and large spikes on long-context prompts (8k-24k), with sensitivity to prompt-length distribution changes. Redwood walked through how the serving runtime splits prefill vs decode regimes, why kernel choice can differ by GPU capability/SM and model family, and how Kernel Auto-Selection v2 aims to make selection deterministic and data-driven (model-family + seq-bucket + GPU normalization) with safe fallbacks and per-family overrides. AcmeAI requested an ability to pin kernels during evaluation and clearer guidance on mixed GPU pools and MIG. Redwood committed to share a selection telemetry guide, run a benchmark sweep on AcmeAI prompt distributions, and propose a dedicated pilot configuration and rollout guardrails.

Fireflies.ai - Transcript

Title: AcmeAI x Redwood - runtime performance deep dive (latency variance / long-context)
Date: 2026-02-14
Time: 10:47 AM - 11:44 AM (PT)
Duration: 57 minutes
Attendees: Ava Chen, Grace Kim, Omar El-Sayed, Yuki Sato, Nadia Rahman, Sarah Klein, Priya Nair, Daniel Cho, Miguel Santos

---

[00:00] Ava Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for making time. This is the deeper performance session we talked about. Goal today is to understand the variance you’re seeing across GPUs and with long context, and then we’ll outline what we can do in the runtime, including kernel selection and rollout controls.

[00:18] Sarah Klein: Sounds good.

[00:20] Ava Chen: Quick intros? I’m Ava, I run the AcmeAI account on our side.

[00:25] Grace Kim: Grace, I lead kernel selection work in the runtime.

[00:29] Omar El-Sayed: Omar, runtime integration and scheduler boundary stuff.

[00:32] Yuki Sato: Yuki, GPU behavior and SKU normalization.

[00:35] Nadia Rahman: Nadia, cost/latency attribution, I look at token-level breakdowns.

[00:41] Priya Nair: Priya, platform engineering at AcmeAI. I own the inference gateway and routing.

[00:47] Daniel Cho: Daniel, ML infra. I’m closer to model configs and quantization experiments.

[00:52] Miguel Santos: Miguel, SRE. I’m the one staring at p95 graphs at 2am.

[00:56] Ava Chen: Great. Priya, do you want to start with what you’re seeing?

[01:02] Priya Nair: Yeah. We’ve got mixed GPUs across environments. In prod we have mostly L4s right now. In staging we still have A10s. And then we test on A100s in our lab. We see like, huge swings in tail latency, and it’s not just the GPU raw speed.

[01:20] Priya Nair: The main complaint internally is that when prompt length distribution shifts, like we go from mostly 1k-2k prompts to suddenly 8k or 12k because a customer enables “document mode”, p95 goes sideways and it’s worse on A10 by a lot.

[01:38] Miguel Santos: And to be precise, p50 is usually fine. It’s the p95 and p99 spikes. Some are like 2-3x, not subtle.

[01:48] Grace Kim: Got it. And you’re seeing this on the same model and same runtime version, just different GPU pools?

[01:53] Priya Nair: Yep. Same model family, same quant. We’re testing Qwen-ish and also a Llama-ish thing. Sorry, I don’t remember the exact naming. But it’s the same artifact.

[02:06] Daniel Cho: For the long prompts, it’s mostly prefill time. Decode is like 100-300 tokens. Prefill is like 8k, sometimes 16k. Rarely 24k.

[02:17] Omar El-Sayed: That matches typical “prefill dominates” regime. One thing we’ve learned is kernel choice that’s good for short context can be pretty bad for long prefill, and vice versa.

[02:28] Sarah Klein: Can you just explain why the same code path would pick different kernels? I think that’s the part we’re not fully trusting.

[02:36] Grace Kim: Yeah. So today our runtime has a selector that chooses attention/prefill/decode kernels. Historically it was more heuristic: detect some model properties, check basic GPU capability, then pick from a set.

[02:51] Grace Kim: The problem is, heuristics get brittle. New GPU SKUs appear, model families change flags like grouped-query attention, and then you get surprising tail behavior.

[03:02] Grace Kim: Kernel auto-selection v2 is our work to make this explicit: inputs are (1) model family, (2) sequence length bucket—separating prefill vs decode—and (3) normalized GPU type. Then we choose a kernel id from a table/registry, with deterministic fallback.

[03:20] Miguel Santos: When you say “sequence length bucket”, do you mean total context or just prompt?

[03:24] Omar El-Sayed: Both, kind of. We label the regime. Prefill uses prompt length heavily. Decode uses “effective context” because KV cache grows. But we bucket it so we don’t explode cardinality.

[03:37] Nadia Rahman: And from an observability standpoint, we also want to answer: was this request “prefill short”, “prefill long”, “decode short”, “decode long”, rather than raw token counts on every metric.

[03:49] Priya Nair: OK. Right now our dashboards don’t show that split clearly. We see “latency” as one number.

[03:56] Ava Chen: This is where we can help. We can share the fields we expose in traces and metrics so you can correlate.

[04:03] Daniel Cho: What’s the risk here though? Like, if kernel selection is wrong, do we get incorrect outputs? Or only perf?

[04:10] Grace Kim: Both are possible. Mostly it manifests as perf regression, but there are edge cases where a kernel under certain shapes can produce NaNs or overflow. That’s why v2 has a “safe kernel set” fallback and conformance tests.

[04:26] Sarah Klein: We had a NaN incident once with a Triton kernel when we were trying something ourselves. So yeah, sensitive.

[04:33] Grace Kim: Exactly. We treat correctness as a hard gate. Performance selection is only among kernels that pass conformance for the shapes in that bucket.

[04:44] Yuki Sato: And on the GPU side, A10 vs L4 is a common source of surprises because they have different SM capabilities and different sweet spots for certain kernels, especially for long prefill.

[04:56] Miguel Santos: Our A10 environment is older and also sometimes runs in partitioned mode. I think it’s MIG? Or maybe that’s only on A100. Sorry.

[05:05] Yuki Sato: MIG is primarily A100/H100 class, not A10. But you might have partial GPU via virtualization or different power settings. We should confirm exact SKU and driver/CUDA versions too.

[05:16] Priya Nair: We can share driver versions. But to be honest, we want a platform where we don’t have to be GPU archaeologists.

[05:25] Ava Chen: Understood.

[05:27] Grace Kim: To make this concrete, can you tell us: for the long context cases, are you doing batching? Or is it mostly single-request because of latency sensitivity?

[05:37] Priya Nair: We try to batch, but with long prompts batching kind of falls apart because you get queueing and then timeouts.

[05:46] Miguel Santos: We have a 20 second timeout at the gateway. Long prompts sometimes eat 12-15 seconds prefill, then any queueing pushes it over.

[05:57] Omar El-Sayed: Right, so in that setting the scheduler should classify it as “prefill long” and prefer kernels optimized for that regime, but also be conservative about batching.

[06:08] Daniel Cho: Our other issue is variance within the same GPU type. Like, two L4 nodes, different tail. We suspect thermal or contention.

[06:18] Yuki Sato: Could be. Also could be differences in clocks, or different PCIe topology, or just background workload. But we can at least remove the “wrong kernel for this regime” source of variance.

[06:31] Grace Kim: Can I ask which models? You mentioned Qwen-ish and Llama-ish.

[06:36] Daniel Cho: Qwen 2.5-ish? And for Llama, it’s like a Llama 3 variant, 8B. Both quantized, 4-bit in staging, 8-bit in prod, we’re still deciding.

[06:50] Grace Kim: OK. Those are two distinct families in our taxonomy. They can want different attention kernels, especially with GQA and head dims.

[07:02] Priya Nair: So what does “taxonomy” mean in practice? Do we have to declare it?

[07:08] Grace Kim: We infer it from model metadata. If metadata is missing, we fall back to “unknown family” and pick from a safe conservative set (and we log that we did that). You can also override/pin per model family in Dedicated deployments.

[07:26] Sarah Klein: That last part is important. During evaluation, we want to freeze behavior. We don’t want a random upgrade changes our kernel choice.

[07:34] Ava Chen: Makes sense.

[07:36] Grace Kim: Yeah, so our rollout plan includes feature flags: selector v2 can be enabled per tier/region, and there’s a deterministic fallback to v1. Additionally, per-family overrides exist so you can pin a kernel id.

[07:52] Miguel Santos: When you say “kernel id”, is that something we can see in logs?

[07:56] Nadia Rahman: Yes, but we typically bucket it. We have a “kernel_choice” field in traces, and metrics break down by selector version, GPU type, seq bucket, and model family. We do not attach raw request ids to metrics, obviously.

[08:13] Miguel Santos: That’s fine. I’m more worried about cardinality blow-ups. We’ve been burned.

[08:18] Nadia Rahman: Same. We explicitly control labels so you don’t get a million series. The “seq bucket” is like {short, medium, long, xlong}, not raw tokens.

[08:30] Priya Nair: OK. What’s the ask from us? What do you need to actually diagnose?

[08:36] Omar El-Sayed: Two things: (1) your prompt length distribution and decode length distribution, ideally per endpoint/route; (2) a few representative prompts for short and long context. If you can’t share raw prompts, even token-counted shape metadata is helpful.

[08:54] Daniel Cho: We can share shapes and synthetic prompts. For some customers we can’t share text, but we can create similar-length documents.

[09:02] Grace Kim: That works.

[09:04] Sarah Klein: I want to push on the core question: why is A10 so much worse? Is it just slower, or something about kernel selection?

[09:13] Yuki Sato: A10 is slower, but the “2-3x tail” suggests either (a) different kernel chosen that has pathological behavior for long prefill, (b) memory pressure / KV cache behavior, or (c) scheduler differences / batching.

[09:28] Omar El-Sayed: Also, on A10 we’ve seen cases where an off-by-one in sequence bucketing causes the selector to think it’s in one regime when it’s actually in the next bucket. That can flip kernel choice.

[09:40] Grace Kim: Not saying that’s your issue, but it’s exactly why we made selection decisions observable.

[09:47] Miguel Santos: Is there a way we can ask “why did you pick this kernel” for a given request?

[09:53] Grace Kim: Yes, we have a debug/explain path internally and in Dedicated we can expose an endpoint/CLI output. It prints: selector version, detected model family, seq bucket, GPU normalized type, and the rule/table entry used.

[10:10] Priya Nair: That would be huge for us.

[10:12] Ava Chen: We can include that as part of the pilot.

[10:15] Daniel Cho: What about long context like 32k? We’re not there yet, but roadmap.

[10:21] Grace Kim: We support long context. The practical constraint is which kernels have been conformance tested for those shapes. v2 allows us to add entries per bucket and per GPU as we validate.

[10:35] Nadia Rahman: And from cost perspective, long prefill dominates cost/token too. The “cheap decode” doesn’t matter if prefill is huge.

[10:46] Sarah Klein: Right now we pay too much for “rare long doc” requests. That’s why we’re even having this meeting.

[10:55] Ava Chen: Understood.

[10:57] Priya Nair: Another angle: We have mixed pools. Like, we might have L4 and A10 simultaneously while we migrate. Does Redwood route based on GPU type?

[11:07] Omar El-Sayed: We can, yes. In Dedicated you can choose homogeneous pools ideally. In Hosted we abstract it, but internally we route based on capacity and policies. For your own infra, if you’re using Redwood Private or Dedicated, we can help you keep pools homogeneous per model or at least per route.

[11:26] Miguel Santos: But if it’s mixed, do you see bigger variance?

[11:30] Omar El-Sayed: Yes, because even if mean is OK, the tail depends on which GPU you hit. That’s why per-SKU selection is important, but also why customers often prefer dedicated homogeneous pools for strict SLOs.

[11:45] Sarah Klein: We’re leaning dedicated, but we need evidence.

[11:49] Ava Chen: That’s fair.

[11:51] Grace Kim: If you’re open to it, we can do a benchmark plan: run your distributions on L4/A10/A100/H100 with v1 selector and v2 selector and show deltas.

[12:04] Daniel Cho: Can you compare to vLLM? That’s our baseline.

[12:08] Ava Chen: We can discuss. We typically benchmark within our runtime, but we can provide relative context. We can also help you run apples-to-apples if you can run the harness.

[12:20] Grace Kim: The main thing is: if the variance you see is due to selection decisions, v2 should reduce that without changing your API.

[12:29] Miguel Santos: I’m going to ask a dumb question: what exactly is “prefill kernel” vs “decode kernel”? Isn’t it the same attention op?

[12:37] Grace Kim: Not dumb. It’s the same conceptual op, but the implementation differs because prefill is like processing the whole prompt in one go (big matrix shapes), decode is incremental with KV cache (small batch of tokens but large cache). Optimal kernels differ.

[12:54] Omar El-Sayed: And the scheduler matters: decode tends to be latency-sensitive per token, while prefill can sometimes tolerate batching if you manage queueing.

[13:04] Priya Nair: OK. That maps to what we see: long prompts blow up before we even start streaming.

[13:11] Nadia Rahman: Do you stream tokens to end users?

[13:14] Priya Nair: Yes, but we can’t stream until prefill finishes, obviously.

[13:19] Nadia Rahman: Right, so reducing prefill p95 is directly improving perceived latency.

[13:26] Sarah Klein: What’s the timeline on your selector v2 being available to us?

[13:31] Ava Chen: We can get you on a canary or a dedicated eval with it, but we want to be careful. Grace, can you speak to stability?

[13:40] Grace Kim: We’re in staged rollout. The key part is it’s feature-flagged and we can pin/override. If we see regressions, we can fall back to v1 quickly.

[13:52] Miguel Santos: What are the rollback criteria? Like, if p95 goes up 10%, do you roll back?

[13:58] Grace Kim: Internally we have SLO guardrails and canary monitors. For a pilot, we can agree on thresholds with you. Typically: if p95 regresses beyond a defined budget for key routes, or if error rates or NaN/correctness signals appear, we disable v2.

[14:17] Omar El-Sayed: Also, selection is deterministic, so if we roll back, behavior is consistent and debuggable.

[14:26] Priya Nair: OK.

[14:28] Daniel Cho: Another issue: we saw that for 8k prompts, sometimes the system “thinks” it’s 7.9k and picks one config, then at 8.1k it flips. Is there hysteresis?

[14:40] Omar El-Sayed: Great question. Buckets do have boundaries. We try to pick boundaries aligned with meaningful shape transitions. In v2 we can also smooth by having the same kernel across adjacent buckets if it avoids cliff effects.

[14:57] Grace Kim: And if we find a cliff, we can add an override entry or adjust boundary logic, but we need your distributions to see where those cliffs matter.

[15:08] Miguel Santos: I like that this is explicit. Right now it feels like magic.

[15:12] Ava Chen: That’s the goal.

[15:14] Sarah Klein: Can we talk about acceptance criteria for a pilot? Like what numbers are “good enough.”

[15:20] Nadia Rahman: If you share your current p50/p95 for short and long routes, we can propose a target. Typically we look at: (1) p95 latency improvement or no regression; (2) reduced variance across GPU types; (3) stable cost/token in the long bucket.

[15:36] Priya Nair: For our doc mode route, current p95 is ~14 seconds on L4 and ~22 seconds on A10. p50 is like 9 and 12.

[15:46] Grace Kim: That’s a big gap.

[15:48] Yuki Sato: Yep. Suggests either kernel mismatch or system-level differences.

[15:54] Daniel Cho: For short route, like chat, p95 is 1.8 seconds L4, 2.2 A10, not huge.

[16:02] Omar El-Sayed: That’s consistent: long prefill path is where you’re paying.

[16:07] Sarah Klein: If we could get A10 closer to L4, or at least predictable, we’d be happy.

[16:14] Ava Chen: Understood.

[16:16] Grace Kim: Do you have any instrumentation that tells you whether you’re memory bound? Like GPU utilization, HBM, etc.

[16:23] Miguel Santos: We have basic GPU util and memory, but it’s noisy. During spikes, util drops sometimes, which is confusing.

[16:31] Omar El-Sayed: That can happen if you’re waiting on CPU side, or if you’re in a less efficient kernel where occupancy is poor.

[16:40] Grace Kim: Another data point: do you see increased errors during spikes? Timeouts? Or only slower.

[16:46] Miguel Santos: Mostly timeouts at the gateway. Sometimes retries cause thundering herd.

[16:52] Priya Nair: That’s why we want to pin behavior during the trial.

[16:57] Ava Chen: We hear you.

[17:00] Daniel Cho: Can you talk about how you detect model family? We have some custom configs.

[17:06] Grace Kim: We look at architecture fields, attention type flags (GQA/MQA), head dim, and sometimes config keys that correlate with family. If it doesn’t match known rules, we mark unknown. You can also provide a mapping in config for your model ids.

[17:24] Priya Nair: So if we have a “frankenmodel” you might treat it unknown.

[17:28] Grace Kim: Yes, but unknown is safe; it may not be optimal.

[17:34] Sarah Klein: That’s acceptable for correctness, but we’ll want to tune it.

[17:39] Grace Kim: Exactly. For enterprise pilots we often add a registry entry after we validate.

[17:45] Ava Chen: We can do that work jointly if the pilot justifies it.

[17:49] Miguel Santos: You mentioned telemetry fields. What would we see?

[17:53] Nadia Rahman: In traces you’d see something like: selector_version=v2, model_family=qwen, seq_bucket=prefill_long, gpu=L4, kernel_id=attn_fa2_v3 (example), plus whether fallback happened.

[18:10] Miguel Santos: And sampling? Because traces at 100% is not possible.

[18:14] Nadia Rahman: We can do sampling, and we can also emit aggregate metrics without request ids.

[18:20] Priya Nair: OK.

[18:22] Sarah Klein: This is helpful. I want to be mindful of time. What do we decide today?

[18:28] Ava Chen: I propose we align on next steps: you send prompt distributions + a few representative prompts/shapes; we run a benchmark sweep and come back with recommendations: dedicated vs hosted canary, plus whether selector v2 + pinning solves variance.

[18:44] Priya Nair: Works.

[18:46] Daniel Cho: One more question: Do you support an “emergency kill switch” if we see a regression?

[18:51] Grace Kim: Yes. It’s effectively disable v2 selector and revert to v1, and you can also pin a safe kernel set.

[18:59] Miguel Santos: Great.

[19:02] Yuki Sato: Can I quickly confirm your A10? Is it A10G (AWS) or on-prem A10?

[19:08] Priya Nair: It’s AWS A10G in staging. L4 is GCP in prod.

[19:14] Yuki Sato: OK, cloud differences can matter too. We normalize GPU types but we also track driver stack.

[19:22] Omar El-Sayed: And network/storage differences, but since you’re seeing it primarily on prefill compute, still likely kernel/scheduler.

[19:31] Sarah Klein: Are you comfortable supporting cross-cloud? We might end up in AWS for compliance.

[19:37] Ava Chen: Yes, we have customers doing that. Dedicated capacity is usually per cloud region, but we can plan.

[19:45] Priya Nair: For now we just need to solve the tail.

[19:49] Grace Kim: Great. If you can share: (a) prompt length histogram; (b) decode length histogram; (c) concurrency profile; and (d) any “doc mode” specifics like max context.

[20:04] Daniel Cho: We’ll send.

[20:06] Miguel Santos: And I’ll send screenshots of the p95 spikes with node labels.

[20:11] Nadia Rahman: Perfect.

[20:13] Ava Chen: OK. Before we wrap, any procurement/security blockers? Not really for this session, but just checking.

[20:21] Sarah Klein: Not yet. If we go dedicated, we’ll ask about audit logs and KMS, but later.

[20:27] Ava Chen: Sounds good.

[20:29] Grace Kim: One last thing: for long context, are you using rope scaling or any special config?

[20:35] Daniel Cho: We do have rope scaling on one model.

[20:38] Grace Kim: OK, note that can shift effective attention behavior. We’ll account for it in model family detection if needed.

[20:46] Priya Nair: Cool.

[20:48] Ava Chen: Great. Let’s schedule the follow-up working session for next week. I’ll send times.

[20:55] Sarah Klein: Thanks all.

[20:56] Miguel Santos: Thanks.

[20:57] Daniel Cho: Thank you.

[20:58] Priya Nair: Yep, thanks.

---
